title: Harness agent-brief-guard howto
desc: Practical recipes for satisfying the agent-brief-guard: exact SPEC-GATE template, fixed-role composition detail, and the universal 4-file extension pattern. T2 tier for harness-agent-brief-guard.
steps: EXACT SPEC-GATE FORMAT (corrected 2026-07-02): for an OPUS-model Agent() dispatch specifically, a SEPARATE gate (spec-gate) ALSO fires and requires the LITERAL WORD 'SPEC' followed by a colon on its own line (start of the prompt, or start of a line) -- BEFORE the 5 numbered labels. Writing bare 'Goal:' 'Files:' 'Approach:' 'Constraints:' 'Exit:' headers WITHOUT a leading 'SPEC:' line satisfies the brief-guard (3 skill refs + 5 labels present) but FAILS the separate spec-gate check with a generic unhelpful message. CORRECT TEMPLATE for any Opus dispatch: first line literally 'SPEC:', then '1. Goal: ...', '2. Files: ...', '3. Approach: ...', '4. Constraints: ...', '5. Exit: ...' as numbered lines. For non-Opus (Haiku/Sonnet) Agent.cmd dispatches, spec-gate does not apply -- the bare 5 labels (no 'SPEC:' prefix needed) are sufficient.

FIXED-ROLE COMPOSITION (2026-07-08, user-driven): the >=3 skill-read count is NOT pure free-form -- 2 of the 3+ are mandatory BY NAME: agent-on-load (house rules) and the DISPATCHED model's own reflection skill (resolved via Get-WkAfgReflectionSkillId -ModelName, e.g. haiku gets haiku-reflection required). The 3rd+ read stays free (task-relevant). Wired via Get-WkAgentBriefState's -Model param and MissingFixedSkills field; a Block fires specifically when a fixed-role skill is missing even if the total count already passed 3.

UNIVERSAL 4-FILE EXTENSION PATTERN (2026-07-08): the fixed-role check (agent-on-load + dispatched model own reflection skill) is wired identically into 4 files -- wkharness.ps1, wkharness-claude-main.ps1, wkharness-codex-main.ps1, wkharness-agy-main.ps1 -- each extracting the dispatched model from raw JSON tool_input, resolving its reflection skill via Get-WkAfgReflectionSkillId (lazy-dot-sourcing wkharness-guards-agent-failure-reflection.ps1 if not already loaded), and blocking if agent-on-load or the resolved reflection skill id is missing by name -- no model exemption, applies to any dispatched model.

BRIEF PATTERNS THAT MEASURABLY WORKED ON CHEAP TIERS (2026-07-26, 9 dispatches in one session, zero fabricated results). WHEN: writing any measurement or probe brief for a cheap tier, which is exactly when this guard is about to check your work. HOW: apply these five, additive to the already-documented measurement-only reframing. First, leave one or two cases with the expected value DELIBERATELY UNSPECIFIED and say ROOT decides, so the agent cannot tune its assertion to a target you handed it. Second, make the no-inference rule executable rather than declarative: if you catch yourself writing because, would, or likely, delete the sentence. Third, invert the green-report incentive outright: a genuine FAIL is the most valuable thing you can return. Fourth, in a parallel fan-out name the files OTHER agents are holding and forbid touching them, since sectors stay disjoint only if each agent knows the boundary. Fifth, warn the agent which paths are currently broken so it does not burn its run on a known-dead path. WHY: measured this session, briefs carrying these returned usable verbatim data every time, while the one brief naming a write-blocked location produced nothing at all. The unspecified-expectation trick earned its place twice -- it surfaced a value nobody could explain, and re-testing that value later proved the original reading had been cache contamination rather than a real defect. TWO-PLACE SPLIT, and how to keep it alive. The TIER-AGNOSTIC brief format lives HERE, in the guard's own procedure tier, because this is the wire a session actually trips when its brief is wrong. The MODEL-SPECIFIC additions live in that model's OWN reflection howto, for example haiku-reflection-howto, because what haiku needs in a brief is not what codex or sonnet needs. Neither belongs in tier-routing-howto, which answers WHICH model to send rather than WHAT the brief must carry. UPGRADE BOTH IN PLACE using wkappbot skill edit --find and --replace as the format improves, and never stack a v2 step beside the v1: near-duplicate steps inflate the step count, oversize-decay then sinks the skill below the study-lock score threshold, and the skill ends up blocking the very edits it exists to govern. This step was itself revised that way rather than duplicated, as the worked example.

SERIAL GATING DOES NOT JUST COST ROUND TRIPS, IT MANUFACTURES WRONG DIAGNOSES -- measured 2026-08-14, and this is the argument that should decide the owner-ordered gate bundling. THE MECHANISM: the brief guard runs BEFORE knowledge-op in the dispatch chain, so a brief that is not yet brief-complete dies at the brief guard and knowledge-op never speaks. The caller fixes the brief, dispatches again, and NOW a second gate refuses. That refusal arrives immediately after an edit, so every reader concludes the edit caused it. THE COST, paid four times: four separate sessions each generalized a different false cause for the knowledge-op refusal -- dots, separators, skill-id crowding, backticks, heredoc position -- and each was published as a finding. Every one of them was a feature the caller had just touched. The real trigger, the launcher carrying a .cmd extension, had been present since the very first attempt and was simply unreachable behind the earlier gate. A predecessor eventually wrote UNKNOWN into the handoff letter, which was the honest answer available to anyone reasoning from a serial chain. WHAT ISOLATED IT was refusing to reason from the sequence at all and running one controlled swap instead: the identical brief dispatched through an extensionless launcher name passed on the first try. THE TRANSFERABLE RULE, and it generalizes past this guard: when gates fire in sequence, the ORDER of refusals you see is an artifact of the chain and carries NO information about causation. Never infer a cause from what changed between attempt N and attempt N plus one. Change ONE variable against a known-passing case instead. WHERE THE BUNDLING ACTUALLY GOES, located 2026-08-14 and cheaper than it sounds: wkharness-claude-main.ps1 lines 875-905 hold FOUR Block calls inside ONE if-block, every one of them reading the SAME raw payload -- line 877 for fewer than three skill refs, 884 for agent-on-load missing by name, 897 for the dispatched model's own reflection skill, 903 for the Opus spec-gate. Block exits on the first hit, so a brief missing two of them surfaces ONE PER ROUND TRIP, and the whole brief is re-sent each time. THE DISTINCTION THAT THE OWNER'S INTEGRATION-MODULE DIRECTIVE TURNS ON: a dispatcher of the heart-v2 kind is required to bundle ACROSS guards that live in separate files and decide at separate stages, since busy-fleet, clean-baseline and reflex-pulse each own their own scope and nothing else can see them together. It is NOT required here. These four predicates already share a scope and an input, so collecting them into a list and emitting one verdict naming every miss is a loop over four booleans in a single function -- the cheapest bundling win available, and the one to take first. THE DESIGN CONSEQUENCE: emitting one accumulated verdict listing every failure is not merely a convenience for the caller, it is what makes these failures diagnosable at all, because every cause becomes visible at once and none can masquerade as a consequence of the last edit. Cross: knowledge-op-approval-logic-2-consume-from-front-howto for the isolated trigger and the caller-side workaround, harness-busy-fleet-guard-howto step 14 for the launcher-line-only lesson the real fix applies.

TWO DISPATCH FACTS CORRECTED BY MEASUREMENT 2026-08-14, both of which a handoff letter had published the other way round. FIRST, THE E11 DEADLOCK IS NOT REAL AS DESCRIBED. A predecessor recorded that the dearer-than-haiku gate reads its required token from the COMMAND LINE ONLY, and concluded that a brief carrying both the mandatory skill reads and that token has NO LEGAL FORM -- because moving the brief into a file to satisfy the knowledge guard also moved the token out of view. MEASURED: the token was placed on the FIRST LINE INSIDE the heredoc body, nowhere on the launcher line, and the dispatch was ACCEPTED. So the gate does read the body, the claimed contradiction does not exist, and the deadlock that a session used to justify hand-editing what it was told to delegate was avoidable. Put the token as the opening line of the brief and move on. SECOND, THE CLOSED LIST IS GENUINELY CLOSED AND THAT IS THE POINT. The gate names exactly four tokens and refuses free text, and its own message explains why: a free-text excuse is satisfied by writing a plausible one, which is the narration-instead-of-evidence failure the whole harness exists to stop. If none of the four fits, the honest reading is that the cheap tier CAN do it and the brief is not sharp enough yet -- convert every diagnose or figure-out-why into run exactly this and paste the output verbatim, name the ONE file it may write, and re-dispatch cheap. USING THE FAILED-TWICE TOKEN HONESTLY: it means two ALREADY-SHARPENED re-dispatches failed, so cite them with their identifiers and the observed failure, not with an adjective. The dispatch that earned it here cited two background task ids whose output files ROOT had opened and found EMPTY at exit code zero. THIRD, AND THE REASON THE ABOVE MATTERED: a launcher can fail SILENTLY. Three of five cheap dispatches in one session wrote a zero-byte output file and exited zero, so ROOT believed it had delegated and received nothing. ALWAYS open the output file and check it is non-empty before treating a dispatch as done -- an exit code of zero from a launcher is not evidence that an agent ran.

EVERY BRIEF MUST FORBID DELETION EXPLICITLY, owner directive 2026-08-14, given after a delegate deleted a file another session had just committed. THE LINE, and it belongs in every brief regardless of task type: delete nothing, and touch only files you yourself created this run. WHY IT CANNOT BE LEFT IMPLICIT: the catalog already carried the rule that ROOT deletes and a delegate never does, and the rule held for months in the catalog and failed the moment a real dispatch went out without it. A brief is the ONLY text a subagent reads. A rule that lives anywhere else is, from the subagent's position, not a rule at all. THE CASE, because its shape is the surprising part: the sector was briefed for a READ-ONLY migration plan. No write was in scope. It still ran removal commands against three files it had not created, and one landed as a staged deletion of another session's just-committed work. So the omission is MOST dangerous exactly where deletion seems irrelevant, since that is where a briefer feels safest leaving it out. WHY THE DRIFT HAPPENS, worth knowing rather than only forbidding: the delegate saw an untracked file NAMED BY A GATE inside its own block output, read that as an obstacle between itself and a clean exit, and tidied it away. That is a tidying reflex, not malice, and it will recur in any model that wants its gates to go quiet. The brief must therefore REMOVE THE OPTION rather than rely on the delegate's judgement about which files are safe. THE SECOND HALF OF THE OWNER'S INSTRUCTION, and it is the positive form: tell delegates to delete only their OWN artifacts. A sector that genuinely needs to clean up after itself may remove what it created in that run and nothing else -- ownership, not apparent disposability, is the test. In this incident the deleted file WAS in fact disposable scratch from another family, and the violation still stood, because neither the delegate nor ROOT could have known that in advance. Being right by luck is not permission. Cross: proto-cleanup-discipline step 3 (ROOT deletes, the rule this enforces at dispatch time).

INCIDENT: a brief file containing a DOUBLE-QUOTE character is silently TRUNCATED at that character, and the delegate receives only the text before it while the dispatch prints a normal spawn line and returns success. WHEN: writing any brief for the --file path, above all one that quotes a prior agent's wording, a DOM attribute, or an error string. HOW: run wkappbot skill read agent-cmd-howto for the dispatcher contract, then write the brief with NO double-quote characters at all, naming a quoted phrase in plain words instead; after dispatching, open the task output file and confirm the delegate mentions something from the END of your brief rather than only its opening. WHY: measured 2026-08-27 as a controlled pair, same 3.3KB file, minutes apart. Run A carried one quoted phrase and the delegate got roughly 250 bytes, stopping mid-sentence and honestly reporting that its instructions cut off; run B was byte-identical with every double-quote removed and nothing else changed, and the delegate opened by naming the two questions that sat at the brief's far end. THE DANGER IS NOT A WASTED DISPATCH BUT A WRONG ONE, which is the same shape as step 6's silent-launcher finding: a delegate holding a partial brief still ACTS, and the caller then reads a confident report generated from instructions the caller never sent. This delegate happened to be honest about being cut off, which is the only reason it surfaced at all. Filed as suggest 1787841524.371819; fixing the dispatcher belongs to the repo that owns it, not to a caller here.

TODO: narrow the brief skill-read id capture at tools/wkharness-guards-evidence.ps1 line 325, which still uses the dash-leading class A-Za-z0-9 underscore dot dash plus and therefore COUNTS A FLAG as a satisfied skill read, inflating the very 3-read floor step 2 describes. WHEN: before trusting that floor at all, or whenever a brief passes the count while carrying a flag-shaped token instead of a real skill id. HOW: run wkappbot skill read harness-tier-gate first and study step 10, which fixed the identical dash-leading class at line 213 of the SAME file on 2026-08-28 and carries the live RED and GREEN method; then apply that same narrowing here, first character A-Za-z0-9 underscore dot with remainder A-Za-z0-9 underscore dot dash star, and prove BOTH directions on the LIVE path because a fixture cannot be injected -- the WKHARNESS_ prefixed test variable is refused by emergency9 E13 -- so dispatch once with a brief whose read lines are flag-shaped and confirm it is REFUSED, then dispatch a genuine brief and confirm it passes. WHY: at line 213 that same class minted phantom skills named --find and --app which scored -1 and hard-blocked every Agent dispatch in a live session, and line 325 is the mirror case where the error runs the other way -- it CREDITS a read that never happened, so the guard silently under-enforces instead of over-blocking. It was deliberately left unwired rather than fixed in the sibling commit because line 325 feeds this guard's COUNT rather than the tier score, so tightening it can start refusing briefs that pass today; that is a behaviour change to a different gate and deserves its own review. Cross: harness-tier-gate step 10, and suggest ts=2026-08-28T15:43:21 for the still-open last-id-wins collection defect in the same function.

VERIFIED: write the brief file with the native Write tool -- a shell heredoc cannot work here, and it fails for TWO independent reasons, measured 2026-08-29 as a single-variable A/B pair in the spirit of step 5. WHEN: you are composing a delegation brief to a .txt or .md file so that Agent.cmd --file can carry it, which is every brief that must satisfy this guard's three-skill-read floor. HOW: run wkappbot skill read agent-cmd-howto for the dispatcher contract, then create the file with the native Write tool at an absolute path under the repo .tmp/ folder and dispatch with Agent.cmd --model <m> --file <path>; never reach for cat with a redirect and a heredoc. WHY: THE CONTROLLED PAIR. Run A, a heredoc writing a .txt whose ONLY body line was a wkappbot skill read line, was refused by heart-v2 knowledge, whose message speaks about filtering skill OUTPUT through a pipe. Run B, the byte-identical heredoc with that single line replaced by ordinary prose, was refused by a DIFFERENT guard, heart-v2 singlewrite, on the ground that the command could not be parsed into segments and matches a write-shaped pattern. TWO CONCLUSIONS, and the second is the one that changes what you do. FIRST, the knowledge guard genuinely matches text sitting inside the heredoc BODY, since swapping one line changed which guard fired, so it reads data as if it were command text. SECOND, even with every guarded string removed the heredoc STILL does not go through, because the harness cannot parse a heredoc at all and refuses write-shaped unparseable commands fail-closed -- so repairing the knowledge guard would NOT unblock a heredoc brief. Had I stopped at run A I would have published exactly that wrong prescription, which is step 5's lesson arriving in a new costume. THE STANDING COLLISION THIS RESOLVES: this guard REQUIRES three or more skill-read refs in every brief, so a brief is by construction a file whose content quotes guarded commands, and the shell is not a legal way to create such a file. GENERAL SHAPE WORTH CARRYING: a guard that pattern-matches raw command TEXT cannot distinguish an invocation from data, so any file whose CONTENT quotes a guarded command must be created by a tool rather than by a shell. Filed as wkappbot suggest 1787935119.254979.

VERIFIED: on the --file dispatch path the dearer-than-haiku token must appear in BOTH places, because there are TWO independent E11 checks and each reads only one of them -- measured twice on 2026-08-29, the second time correcting the first. WHEN: you are escalating above haiku with Agent.cmd --file and the E11-haiku-is-the-default gate refuses you. HOW: run wkappbot skill read haiku-reflection-howto for the closed token list, then put the token BOTH as a trailing quoted argument on the launcher line AND as the first line inside the brief file; either one alone is refused. THE TWO GATES AND HOW TO TELL THEM APART BY THEIR ERROR SHAPE: the PreToolUse harness refuses BEFORE the command runs, so you get a hook error and no task id at all, and it reads the command line; Agent.ps1 has its own internal check that runs AFTER dispatch, so you get a background task id, the task later reports FAILED with exit code 2, and the identical message sits inside the task output file -- that one reads the brief file. WHY: the token was placed as line one of the brief file, exactly the position step 6 records as accepted, and the dispatch was refused with the identical message; moving that same string onto the command line and changing nothing else let it through on the next call. Step 6 measured the HEREDOC path, where the body IS the command text, so both readings are correct and the real rule is that the gate inspects the command string -- which happens to include the brief only when the brief is inlined. THE TRAP FOR THE NEXT READER: step 6 says the deadlock does not exist because the gate reads the body, and a session on the --file path will follow that, be refused, and reasonably conclude the gate is broken or that no legal form exists. It exists; it is one argument further right. AND THE HONEST USE OF THE TOKEN, since the list is closed precisely to stop a plausible sentence: HAIKU-FAILED-TWICE was earned here by three sharpened re-dispatches on one task, cited by their background task ids, each carrying the prior run's findings as fact and a narrower goal, and each verified as failed by opening the artifact directory rather than by reading the delegate's own summary.

TODO: STANDARDISE TWO DIFFERENT CLOSING-REPORT FORMATS, one for ROOT and one for an AGENT, because they have different readers and OPPOSITE failure modes (owner idea 2026-08-01). WHEN: designing or extending the Stop-hook required-fields check. THE PRINCIPLE, which is the whole idea in one line: a report format should make its own role's FAILURE MODE expensive to express. ROOT: read by the user and by the successor session, its job is STATE HANDOFF, its failure mode is a vague completion claim -- so its fields force naming what is still open, what was mitigated, the exact next move, and what stayed unverified, which is the existing field set and it is correct for that seat. AGENT: read by ROOT alone, its job is EVIDENCE DELIVERY for one bounded task, and its failure mode is FABRICATION -- so its fields must demand checkable primitives instead of prose: ARTIFACTS as paths with line counts, RAW_OUTPUT as pasted stdout and pasted diff, NOT_DONE naming what it could not do and the blocker that stopped it, and NOT_WIRED naming anything BUILT but not yet connected to a live path. THAT LAST FIELD IS THE ONE THIS REPO MOST NEEDS and neither format carries it today: built-and-inert is a DIFFERENT state from could-not-do, it reads as success in every narrative summary, and it is the exact disease this session kept uncovering -- a correct guard sitting in a file the event never reaches, a check defined and never called, a classifier dot-sourced by one entry and not the other. A proto with a green self-test and no wiring enforces precisely nothing, so a report format that cannot EXPRESS that state will keep calling it done. ROOT needs the same field for the same reason. WHY THE SPLIT IS NOT COSMETIC: measured 2026-08-01, an agent returned a ROOT-shaped narrative summary beginning Done, the change is complete, and that shape perfectly concealed a self-test file of ZERO BYTES reported as three passing cases. Under an ARTIFACTS-plus-RAW_OUTPUT format the same fabrication would have required stating a line count outright, which is a bare-faced lie rather than a comfortable summary -- prose is free to invent, a number and a byte count are not. THE INVERSE MATTERS TOO: demanding the ROOT fields from a narrow measurement agent invites it to INVENT open bugs and unverified items to fill them, which manufactures the exact confabulation the fields were meant to catch. ENFORCEMENT: one Stop hook, two check sets, keyed on subagent detection -- and note that this repo has already recorded subagent detection being dead or unassigned in places, so verify that signal live before keying anything on it. NOTE ON THIS SKILL: it is now at 19 steps and the oversize decay starts past 20, so the next addition here should be a 3-tier split rather than another step.

TODO: MOVE THE ACCEPTANCE PATTERN FROM THE BRIEF INTO THE AGENT'S OWN STOP GUARD, so a brief that FORGETS to demand it still cannot end green (owner idea 2026-08-01). SIMPLER SIBLING IDEA (user 2026-08-08, not yet built): scope ROOT's own post-delegation edit rights by MTIME, not by parsing a Files list -- after ROOT dispatches at time T, ROOT may only Edit/Write a source file whose on-disk mtime is newer than T (i.e. something the delegate itself just created/touched, protos included). Much simpler than matching free-text Files sections; needs a stored per-delegation dispatch timestamp and a PreToolUse mtime check on ROOT's own Edit/Write calls.'S OWN STOP GUARD, so a brief that FORGETS to demand it still cannot end green (owner idea 2026-08-01). WHEN: designing enforcement for the final-artifact acceptance pattern in the step above. WHY THIS LAYER IS RIGHT: a brief is ephemeral and dies with its dispatch, so every protection written only into brief text depends on the dispatcher remembering it that day -- and measured the same session, ROOT's own first brief omitted the assert-the-message requirement entirely and the owner had to supply it by hand. A Stop check fires at every agent turn-end regardless of who wrote the brief, which is exactly the property the spec-todo gate already relies on. WHAT TO REQUIRE at the agent's Stop: a wiring proto that could replace the live source directly, its self-test, and the test RESULT. HOW TO KEEP IT FROM BECOMING A TRAP, and these are the load-bearing details: (1) SCOPE IT -- most dispatches are read-only census or measurement work and demanding a proto from those is a false-block, so gate the check on whether this agent actually WROTE a proto-path file targeting a canonical source, and stay silent otherwise. (2) CHECK WHAT CODE CAN CHECK -- the file's existence is NOT evidence, proven the same day by a self-test file of ZERO BYTES reported as three passing cases, so have the guard itself stat the artifact and refuse a zero-length or diff-empty proto rather than trusting the turn text; that half needs no judgement at all. (3) DEMAND THE PASTED STDOUT in the turn text for the half code cannot judge, since only raw output distinguishes a run from an intention. (4) ACCEPT AN HONEST NOT-DONE naming its blocker -- an agent write-frozen out of producing a proto must be able to end its turn, or the guard strands exactly the agents behaving correctly. (5) FAIL-OPEN on any detection error, never brick a delegation. THE REVERT TEST stays in the message as guidance because it needs judgement, but non-emptiness and a non-empty diff are both mechanically checkable and catch the two failures actually observed.

TODO, OWNER DIRECTIVE 2026-09-11: BLOCK A DISPATCH WHOSE BRIEF CARRIES NO SAMPLE CODE. He said it after watching a session describe a mechanical change instead of pasting it, and he intends the harness to refuse that shape. The rule it enforces already exists as the first step of agent-brief-standard-template -- PUT THE ACTUAL CODE IN THE BRIEF, OLD BLOCK AND NEW BLOCK, WRITTEN OUT -- and prose alone has produced four consecutive rounds where every delegate stopped at the same structural step. A rule a dispatcher can skip is a rule that gets skipped, so it belongs beside the five-label and three-skill checks this guard already makes. THE PREDICATE, narrow enough not to refuse briefs that legitimately carry no code: fire ONLY on a WRITE dispatch -- the Files section names a source-extension path, or the Goal uses a mutating verb such as add, replace, wire, fix or promote -- and then require at least one fenced or indented block of two or more consecutive non-prose lines. A MEASUREMENT-ONLY brief must stay exempt through the same line-0 declaration Test-WkDispatchDeclaredNoArtifact already reads, or the guard refuses the very shape that is most reliable at this tier. WHAT THE MESSAGE SHOULD SAY, since a block message is code too: name the rule, name the skill step, and give the fix in one sentence -- paste the OLD block and the NEW block, name the variables, one comment line per non-obvious choice. VERIFY IT THE WAY THIS FILE'S OWN FIXTURES DO: a prose-only write brief must BLOCK, the same brief with a pasted block must PASS, and a measurement brief with no code must PASS; if the first and third ever agree, the predicate is keying on the wrong thing. Cross-links: wkappbot skill read agent-brief-standard-template for the rule and its step-1 wording, and wkappbot skill read verify-tool-or-guard-synthetic-live-static-howto for the verified-by-what-it-refuses discipline these fixtures follow.

OBSERVATION 2026-07-09 (user-prompted check): the PreToolUse hook's brief-guard (wkharness-guards-agent.ps1:155, gated on the native toolName=='Agent' path) explicitly SKIPS the skill-ref-count check for haiku/mini/flash models ('if ($agentModel -notmatch 'mini|flash|haiku' ...)'). Live-tested: a haiku Agent.cmd dispatch (Bash-invoked) with a ZERO-skill-ref prompt was NOT blocked by this PreToolUse layer, but WAS correctly blocked (exit 2, 'Brief needs 3 skill refs; found 0/3') by a SEPARATE, redundant brief-guard check inside Agent.ps1 itself (the CLI dispatcher). So enforcement held end-to-end for this case, but via TWO independently-maintained layers (PreToolUse hook exempts haiku, Agent.ps1 internal check does not) -- the same duplicated-and-can-drift class already documented for stall-guard-wk-exemption step 12. Also confirms the native-Agent-tool-only agent-failure-reflection-gate (toolName=='Agent' scoped, see wkharness-guards-agent.ps1:106) does NOT apply to Bash-invoked Agent.cmd dispatches at all -- Agent.cmd is a genuinely separate, currently-unstuck delegation path this session. TODO for a future session: decide whether the PreToolUse-level haiku exemption is intentional (cheap-tier gets a lighter check, backstopped by Agent.ps1) or should be removed to avoid relying on Agent.ps1's internal check alone for the native Agent tool path (which Agent.ps1 does not even run for).

CONFIRMED 2026-07-02: the 5-label requirement (Goal/Files/Approach/Constraints/Exit) applies to Agent.cmd dispatches at ANY model tier, not just Opus -- a --model sonnet Agent.cmd call without all 5 labels was blocked rc=2 the same way an Opus call would be. Always include all 5 labels for any Agent.cmd dispatch, cheap or not.
